label: Oscilloscope Setup & Signal Troubleshooting (synthetic sample)
note: Bundled saved demonstration used for the offline path. Transcript is synthetic; replace with a real consented expert recording for the competition demo.

transcript.text: Alright, let's get started. Today I want to show you how I set up the oscilloscope from scratch, and then how I debug a signal that looks unstable on the screen.
First rule before you touch any knob: connect the ground clip first. If you connect the probe tip before ground you can float the scope and damage the front end.
So, ground clip first, then the probe tip onto the test point. Take your time here, because a loose ground clip is the number one cause of ghost noise on the trace.
Now the vertical scale. I know this circuit runs about two volts peak to peak, so I set volts per division to five hundred millivolts.
Why five hundred? Because the screen is eight divisions tall. Two volts needs four divisions, and that leaves headroom for overshoot without clipping the trace.
If the trace disappears off the top of the screen, don't chase it with the position knob. Fix the volts per division first. That is the most common mistake I see beginners make.
Next, the timebase. Our test signal is one kilohertz, which means one full cycle every millisecond.
I set the time division to five hundred microseconds. That gives me exactly two full cycles across the ten horizontal divisions, enough to judge the period and the symmetry.
If the timebase is too fast you only see noise, and too slow the cycles squash together. Two cycles on screen is my rule of thumb.
Now the part everyone skips: triggering. Without a trigger the waveform free-runs and drifts sideways, so nothing you measure will ever repeat.
I enable edge trigger, rising edge, and set the trigger level to about four hundred millivolts, which sits roughly a third of the way up the rising slope.
The level must cross a clean part of the slope. If you park it on the noisy flat top of the waveform, the scope triggers on noise and the display jitters all day.
Okay, now watch what happens when something goes wrong. See the trace drifting? Someone knocked the trigger level off the slope, so the scope lost its lock.
My recovery is always the same three moves: enable the trigger, walk the level down until I see a clean rising crossing, then stop. The trace locks instantly.
And if the trace is still jumpy after that, I check the ground clip before blaming the probe. Nine times out of ten it is the ground. That is the whole routine.

extraction.title: Oscilloscope Setup & Signal Troubleshooting
extraction.summary: A five-step bench routine for bringing an oscilloscope up on a known 1 kHz, 2 Vpp test signal: ground the probe first, set 500 mV/div vertical, 500 µs/div timebase, lock a rising edge trigger at 400 mV, and recover a drifting trace by re-walking the trigger.

steps.title: Connect the ground clip before the probe tip
steps.instructions: Before touching any controls, attach the probe's ground clip to the circuit's ground reference, then place the probe tip on the test point. Confirm the ground clip seats firmly.
steps.rationale: Connecting the tip first can float the scope relative to the circuit and damage the front end; a loose ground is the top cause of ghost noise on the trace.
success_cues: Ground clip seats firmly with no wiggle
Baseline trace shows no ghost noise with tip removed
common_mistakes: Connecting the probe tip before the ground clip
Leaving the ground clip loosely attached
steps.recovery: If unexplained noise appears later, reseat the ground clip first and re-check before suspecting the probe.

evidence.quote: connect the ground clip first. If you connect the probe tip before ground you can float the scope and damage the front end
a loose ground clip is the number one cause of ghost noise

simulator.note: Physical bench action; no simulator task. Watch the explanation and continue.

steps.title: Set vertical scale to 500 mV/div
steps.instructions: Set VOLTS/DIV to 500 mV. The 2 Vpp test signal should occupy about four of the eight vertical divisions, centered on screen.
steps.rationale: Two volts needs four divisions at 500 mV/div, leaving headroom for overshoot without clipping; the screen is eight divisions tall.
success_cues: Waveform peaks stay inside the graticule with visible headroom
Waveform occupies roughly half the screen height
common_mistakes: Chasing an off-screen trace with the position knob instead of fixing VOLTS/DIV
steps.recovery: If the trace runs off the top or bottom, return to VOLTS/DIV and step until the full waveform fits.

evidence.quote: I set volts per division to five hundred millivolts
Two volts needs four divisions, and that leaves headroom for overshoot without clipping
don't chase it with the position knob. Fix the volts per division first

simulator.note: Scope starts mis-set at 5 V/div (waveform nearly flat). Set 500 mV/div.

steps.title: Set timebase to 500 µs/div
steps.instructions: Set TIME/DIV to 500 µs so the 1 kHz signal shows exactly two full cycles across the ten horizontal divisions.
steps.rationale: One kilohertz means one cycle per millisecond; two cycles on screen is enough to judge period and symmetry without squashing or over-zooming.
success_cues: Exactly two full cycles visible across the screen
Rising and falling slopes look symmetric
common_mistakes: Timebase too fast: only noise visible
Timebase too slow: cycles squash together
steps.recovery: Count cycles on screen and adjust TIME/DIV until exactly two cycles fit.

evidence.quote: Our test signal is one kilohertz, which means one full cycle every millisecond
I set the time division to five hundred microseconds
Two cycles on screen is my rule of thumb

simulator.note: Scope starts at 100 µs/div (over-zoomed, one partial cycle). Set 500 µs/div.

steps.title: Enable rising-edge trigger at about 400 mV
steps.instructions: Enable edge trigger, select the rising edge, and set the trigger level to roughly 400 mV — about a third of the way up the rising slope.
steps.rationale: Without a trigger the waveform free-runs and nothing repeats. The level must cross a clean part of the slope; on the noisy flat top the scope triggers on noise and jitters.
success_cues: Trace stops drifting and holds still
Trigger level line sits on the rising slope, not the flat top
common_mistakes: Leaving the trigger disabled and blaming the probe
Parking the level on the noisy flat top of the waveform
steps.recovery: Walk the level down until it crosses a clean rising slope, then stop.

evidence.quote: Without a trigger the waveform free-runs and drifts sideways, so nothing you measure will ever repeat
I enable edge trigger, rising edge, and set the trigger level to about four hundred millivolts
If you park it on the noisy flat top of the waveform, the scope triggers on noise and the display jitters

simulator.note: Trigger starts disabled and the trace free-runs. Enable rising-edge trigger at ~400 mV.

steps.title: Recover a drifting trace
steps.instructions: When the trace drifts: enable the trigger, walk the trigger level down until a clean rising crossing appears, then stop adjusting. If it is still jumpy, reseat the ground clip before blaming the probe.
steps.rationale: A knocked-off trigger level is the usual cause of a drifting trace; the same three recovery moves fix it every time, and the ground clip explains most remaining cases.
success_cues: Trace locks and holds still after the level crosses a clean rising slope
No residual jitter after reseating ground
common_mistakes: Turning random knobs instead of following the three fixed recovery moves
Replacing the probe before checking the ground clip
steps.recovery: Enable trigger -> walk level to a clean rising crossing -> stop; then check ground.

questions.question: Why do you always use the rising edge rather than the falling edge for this signal?
questions.why_missing: The expert consistently selected the rising edge but never explained why it is preferred here.

questions.question: What is your procedure when the signal amplitude is unknown before setting VOLTS/DIV?
questions.why_missing: The expert assumed the known 2 Vpp test signal; the unknown-amplitude case was never covered.

questions.question: How do probe attenuation settings (1x/10x) change the vertical scale you choose?
questions.why_missing: The demonstration used one probe setting without discussing how attenuation affects the mV/div math.
